justification: Formed a fresh judgement first, then checked round 1. Ran the harness myself: node tools/check-article.mjs (PASS, errors=0 warnings=0, words=4566), node tools/run-code.mjs (PASS, blocks=22 executed=11), and node tools/gate.mjs, which passed clean end to end (Lighthouse 100/100/100/100, console=0, brokenLinks=0, overflow=0px). I re-fetched all 9 primary sources live and checked every inline quote and paraphrase against the current page text: CWE-89's definition and its 'Common Consequences' table order, Microsoft's SQL Server injection guide (the 'prematurely terminating a text string', comment-mark, and semicolon-delimiter sentences), OWASP's cheat sheet (the 'fragile... CANNOT guarantee' escaping line, the 'database will always distinguish between code and data' prepared-statement guarantee, and its least-privilege guidance), Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's Parameters, Batching and Connection-strings pages, EF Core's SQL Queries page (the FromSql/FromSqlInterpolated-safe vs FromSqlRaw-vulnerable sentence and the 'databases do not allow parameterizing column names' line), and SQLite's own rescode.html (SQLITE_READONLY) and datatype3.html. On that last one I went past the surface claim and re-derived the actual mechanism: SQLite's comparison-affinity rule (section 4.2, 'Type Conversions Prior To Comparison') is exactly what the article describes -- numeric affinity is applied to a TEXT operand compared against an INTEGER/REAL-affinity column only if the text is a well-formed numeric literal, otherwise no conversion happens and the INTEGER/REAL-vs-TEXT ordering rule (section 4.1) applies -- so the article's claim is not just directionally right but precisely right, including the 'not a coincidence of this one payload' framing. I re-ran the reasoning behind every non-trivial code sample (rowid/insertion-order behavior of the unordered-scan exercise, ExecuteReader/NextResult draining semantics for the stacked-query batches, UNION SELECT column-count compatibility with the two-column account table, Mode=ReadOnly requiring a file-backed database rather than :memory:) and found no error. I fetched two of the query's actual top-ranking competitors, StackHawk's .NET SQL injection guide and Snyk's EF Core injection post, plus Microsoft's own SQL Server injection page (all three already listed in round 1's comparedAgainst, re-verified this round rather than assumed): neither StackHawk nor Snyk runs any executable exploit, neither discusses escaping's specific failure on non-string fields, neither discusses least privilege's actual limit (a read-only connection still leaks data via UNION), and Snyk's FromSqlRaw/FromSqlInterpolated coverage is a one-line mention with no demonstration. This article does all four with real, running code. Round 1's one major finding (the false 'CWE-89 opens with reading confidential data' claim) is genuinely fixed, not papered over: the current text ('it lists "Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands" first and "Read Application Data" second') is exactly correct against CWE-89's live page, which I re-fetched independently rather than trusting the round-1 write-up. Both of round 1's minor findings are also properly fixed: the Batching page is now in front-matter sources and cited inline at the exact sentence describing ExecuteReader/NextResult/Dispose semantics, and the SQLite comparison-affinity rule is now named and cited rather than left as an unexplained outcome. I found no new factual error and no failing code, so nothing caps the score below the 'ships with nits only' band; the remaining gap to a 10 is that the piece is already close to definitive for its scope rather than that anything is wrong with it.
